title: 22. Interview: Reverse Proxy
summary: Interview Q&A for Reverse Proxy — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Reverse Proxy interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is a reverse proxy, and how is it different from a forward proxy?
**Answer:** A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers and accepts incoming client requests, forwarding them to one of several backends, then returning the response to the client. The client thinks it is talking to the server; the server thinks it is talking to a client; neither knows the proxy is there. Use cases: load balancing, TLS termination, caching, rate limiting, routing, observability. Examples: NGINX, Envoy, AWS ALB, Google's GFE. A forward proxy is the opposite — it sits in front of clients and forwards their requests outbound to the internet. The forward proxy hides the client from the server (e.g., a corporate web filter or `squid` at a school); the reverse proxy hides the server from the client. The same software (NGINX, HAProxy) can do both, but the role is opposite: forward proxy = "I am a client, hide me from the server"; reverse proxy = "I am the server, hide my backends from the client." The mnemonic: forward = outbound (proxies on behalf of client), reverse = inbound (proxies on behalf of server).
**Visual:**
```
Forward proxy (client-side):         Reverse proxy (server-side):
  client -> [forward proxy] -> internet   client -> [reverse proxy] -> backend
  +------+ +-------------+ +----------+   +------+ +--------------+ +--------+
  |client| |corporate    | |external  |   |client| |NGINX/ALB     | |backend |
  |      | |web filter   | |server    |   |      | |              | |(hidden)|
  +------+ +-------------+ +----------+   +------+ +--------------+ +--------+
  hides client identity from server       hides backend identity from client
```

### Q2. What load balancing algorithms does a reverse proxy use, and when would you pick each?
**Answer:** The common algorithms: (1) **Round-robin** — each backend in turn; simple, works well when backends are homogeneous and request cost is uniform. (2) **Least-connections** — send to the backend with the fewest in-flight requests; better when request cost varies (e.g., some endpoints are 10x slower than others). (3) **IP-hash / consistent hashing** — hash the client IP (or session ID) to a backend; provides session affinity (the same client always hits the same backend, useful for stateful sessions or local cache hit). Consistent hashing minimizes remapping when backends are added or removed. (4) **Weighted round-robin** — assign each backend a weight proportional to its capacity; useful when backends have different sizes (e.g., 4-core and 8-core instances in the same pool). (5) **Random** — pick a backend at random; surprisingly effective at scale and trivially stateless. (6) **Latency-based** — measure each backend's response time and prefer faster ones; can cause herd behavior if not damped. Pick based on workload: round-robin for homogeneous backends with uniform requests, least-connections for variable request cost, IP-hash for session affinity, weighted for heterogeneous backends. AWS ALB defaults to round-robin; NGINX supports all of these.
**Visual:**
```
Round-robin (homogeneous backends, uniform cost):
  req1 -> B1, req2 -> B2, req3 -> B3, req4 -> B1, ...

Least-connections (variable cost):
  B1 has 3 in-flight, B2 has 1, B3 has 5 -> next req -> B2

IP-hash (session affinity):
  client 10.0.0.5 -> hash -> B2 (always B2 for this client)
  client 10.0.0.9 -> hash -> B1 (always B1 for this client)

Weighted (B1=8 core, B2=4 core, B3=4 core):
  weights: B1=2, B2=1, B3=1
  req -> B1, B2, B1, B3, B1, B2, ...  (B1 gets 50% of traffic)
```

### Q3. How does TLS termination at a reverse proxy work, and what are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** TLS termination means the reverse proxy holds the TLS certificate, completes the TLS handshake with the client, decrypts incoming TLS records, and forwards the resulting plaintext HTTP to the backend over a private network. Benefits: (1) CPU offload — asymmetric crypto (RSA/ECDSA signatures) is expensive; consolidating it on the proxy lets backends focus on application logic. (2) Centralized cert management — one cert on the proxy instead of N certs across N backends; renewal happens in one place. (3) Protocol flexibility — the proxy can accept HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 from clients while forwarding HTTP/1.1 to legacy backends. (4) Inspection — the proxy can read the plaintext to apply routing, caching, and WAF rules. Trade-offs: (1) **Trust boundary** — the proxy can see all decrypted traffic; if compromised, the attacker has plaintext. For sensitive data (banking, healthcare), use end-to-end TLS (proxy re-encrypts to backend, called "Full strict" in Cloudflare). (2) **Single point of cert failure** — if the cert expires or is misconfigured, the entire site breaks. (3) **Latency** — adding the proxy adds a hop, though this is ~1 ms on a LAN. (4) **Compliance** — some regulations (PCI-DSS, HIPAA) require end-to-end encryption with no plaintext hop. The standard pattern is "TLS termination at edge + TLS to backend," giving you edge offload without an unencrypted hop.
**Visual:**
```
TLS termination at proxy (CPU offload, plaintext to backend):
  client --TLS--> proxy --HTTP (plaintext)--> backend
  + cert on proxy, plaintext on LAN (only OK inside VPC)

End-to-end TLS (re-encrypt to backend):
  client --TLS--> proxy --TLS--> backend
  + cert on proxy AND cert on backend
  + plaintext never on wire (even inside VPC)
  - more CPU on backend (negligible if backend count > 1)

mTLS to backend (zero-trust):
  client --TLS--> proxy --mTLS--> backend
  + backend verifies proxy identity via client cert
  + zero-trust: even inside VPC, no implicit trust
```

### Q4. How do health checks work in a reverse proxy, and why do you need both active and passive?
**Answer:** Active health checks are the proxy periodically polling each backend's health endpoint (e.g., `GET /health` every 5 seconds) and removing unhealthy backends from the pool. NGINX's `health_check interval=5s fails=3 passes=2`, AWS ALB's target group health checks, and Envoy's active health checks all do this. The trade-off: 5-second polling means a backend can serve traffic for up to 5 seconds after it fails. Passive health checks (also called "circuit breaking" or "outlier detection") watch real traffic: if a backend returns N consecutive 5xx errors or timeouts, the proxy marks it unhealthy and stops sending traffic. Envoy's outlier detection, AWS ALB's " unhealthy threshold", and HAProxy's "observe layer7" all do this. Passive checks react in milliseconds (within the failure window), while active checks confirm recovery more reliably. Use both: passive for fast reaction to failure, active for fast detection of recovery. The health endpoint should reflect real health — checking the backend can reach its database, not just that the process is up. A common pitfall: a `/health` endpoint that always returns 200, so the proxy never removes a failing backend. Netflix's Hystrix popularized the "circuit breaker" pattern: if a backend exceeds an error threshold, open the circuit and stop sending traffic for a cooldown period, then probe with a single request to test recovery.
**Visual:**
```
Active health check (poll every 5s):
  proxy -> GET /health every 5s -> backend
  3 consecutive failures -> mark unhealthy, remove from pool
  2 consecutive passes -> mark healthy, re-add to pool

Passive health check (observe real traffic):
  req1 -> B1 -> 500 (failure count: 1)
  req2 -> B1 -> 500 (failure count: 2)
  req3 -> B1 -> 500 (failure count: 3) -> trip circuit, stop sending to B1

Combined:
  passive catches the failure within milliseconds (3 requests)
  active confirms recovery every 5s after cooldown
```

### Q5. What is path-based routing and host-based routing in a reverse proxy?
**Answer:** Path-based routing forwards different URL paths to different backend pools. NGINX: `location /api/ { proxy_pass http://api_backend; }` and `location /static/ { proxy_pass http://static_backend; }`. AWS ALB: listener rules that route `/api/*` to one target group, `/static/*` to another. Use case: a single domain serving multiple services — `api.example.com/users` goes to the user service, `api.example.com/orders` goes to the order service, all behind one TLS cert and one hostname. Host-based routing forwards different Host headers to different backends — `api.example.com` goes to the API pool, `www.example.com` goes to the web pool, `admin.example.com` goes to the admin pool. NGINX: separate `server` blocks with `server_name`. AWS ALB: listener rules matching the Host header. Use case: a single ALB serving many microsites. Combined: path-based + host-based gives you a routing matrix. Trade-off: as you add more rules, the proxy config grows complex and rule evaluation has a small latency cost (negligible for hundreds of rules, measurable for thousands). API gateways (Phase 8) extend this with method-based routing, header-based routing, and content-based routing (route based on JWT claims). Kubernetes Ingress is a reverse proxy (NGINX Ingress, Traefik, Istio Ingress) that does host- and path-based routing for services inside a cluster.
**Visual:**
```
Host-based routing:
  api.example.com   -> backend pool "api"
  www.example.com   -> backend pool "web"
  admin.example.com -> backend pool "admin"

Path-based routing (within api.example.com):
  /api/users/*  -> user-service
  /api/orders/* -> order-service
  /api/auth/*   -> auth-service
  /static/*     -> cdn-origin (or S3)

AWS ALB listener rule example:
  IF Host = api.example.com AND Path = /api/users/* THEN -> user-tg
  IF Host = api.example.com AND Path = /api/orders/* THEN -> order-tg
  IF Path = /static/* THEN -> static-tg
```

### Q6. What is a service mesh and how does Envoy fit in as a reverse proxy sidecar?
**Answer:** A service mesh is a transparent layer that handles service-to-service communication concerns — mTLS, traffic splitting, circuit breaking, retries, timeouts, observability — without application code changes. The pattern: deploy a reverse proxy (Envoy is the most common) as a sidecar container in every pod. Use iptables to redirect all inbound and outbound traffic through the sidecar. The sidecar terminates mTLS from the upstream sidecar, applies traffic policies (e.g., "10% of calls from billing to orders go to v2"), enforces retries and timeouts, and emits metrics and traces. Istio is the most popular service mesh; Linkerd uses its own Rust proxy. The control plane (Istiod) configures all sidecars via xDS APIs. Benefits: mTLS everywhere with zero application code; consistent observability across all services; canary deploys via traffic splitting without code changes; circuit breaking protects against cascading failures. Trade-offs: (1) resource overhead — ~50 MB RAM and ~5% CPU per pod, which at 10,000 pods is real money; (2) latency — each hop adds 1–2 ms through the sidecar; (3) operational complexity — debugging a request that goes through 4 sidecars (client sidecar, gateway, server sidecar, intermediate sidecars) requires distributed tracing. Netflix, Airbnb, and Square have all adopted service meshes to manage microservice complexity at scale.
**Visual:**
```
Pod (billing service):                Pod (orders service):
  +-----------------------+             +-----------------------+
  | billing app (port 8080)|             | orders app (port 8080)|
  |   ^                   |             |   ^                   |
  |   | loopback          |             |   | loopback          |
  |   v                   |             |   v                   |
  | Envoy sidecar (15001) |<== mTLS ===>| Envoy sidecar (15001) |
  +-----------------------+             +-----------------------+
  iptables redirects                    iptables redirects
  all outbound -> sidecar               all inbound -> sidecar

Sidecar handles: mTLS, traffic splitting, retries, timeouts,
                 circuit breaking, metrics, tracing
Application code: unchanged
```

### Q7. Why might you chain multiple reverse proxies (CDN -> WAF -> ALB -> sidecar)? What are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** A modern production request typically traverses 3–5 reverse proxies: CDN edge (Cloudflare, Akamai) → WAF (Web Application Firewall, also a proxy) → cloud load balancer (AWS ALB) → service mesh ingress → service mesh sidecar → backend. Each layer adds a function: CDN caches static content and absorbs DDoS; WAF filters SQL injection and bad bots; ALB does TLS termination and path-based routing; ingress routes within the cluster; sidecar does mTLS and traffic splitting. The benefit is separation of concerns — each layer is independently configurable, observable, and replaceable. Trade-offs: (1) **Latency** — each hop adds 1–2 ms; 5 hops = 5–10 ms added to every request. Negligible for most apps, material for ultra-low-latency trading. (2) **Debugging** — when a request fails, you need trace headers (W3C Trace Context) propagated through every proxy, plus logs at each layer, to localize the failure. (3) **Header pollution** — each proxy adds headers (X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, Via); if not normalized, the final backend sees a confusing chain. (4) **Configuration drift** — each proxy has its own config (Cloudflare YAML, ALB listener rules, NGINX, Envoy xDS); keeping them consistent requires tooling. (5) **Cost** — each layer has its own pricing (CDN per-GB, ALB per-LCU, sidecar compute). The right number of layers is the minimum that provides the functions you need. For a small service, a single ALB is enough. For a large service with global users and compliance requirements, the full chain is justified.
**Visual:**
```
client -> CDN (Cloudflare) -> WAF -> ALB -> K8s Ingress -> Envoy sidecar -> backend
         |                  |     |     |               |                  |
         caches, DDoS       |     |     |               |                  app
         absorbs 100G       SQLi  TLS   path routing    mTLS, traffic
         scrubbing          filter off  /api -> svc1    splitting

Per-hop cost: 1-2ms latency, 1 config to maintain, 1 set of logs
Total chain: 5 hops = 5-10ms added latency, 5 configs, 5 log streams
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your e-commerce API runs on 3 backend instances behind an NGINX reverse proxy. Users report intermittent 502 errors during peak hours. How do you debug?
**Answer:** A 502 Bad Gateway means NGINX could not get a valid response from a backend — the backend either refused the connection, closed it mid-response, or timed out. Debug steps. (1) **Check NGINX error logs** — `tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log` will show which backend failed and why (connection refused, timeout, premature close). Look for `upstream timed out` (backend too slow) vs `connection refused` (backend down) vs `upstream sent invalid header` (backend returned malformed response). (2) **Check backend health** — `curl` each backend's `/health` endpoint directly; one is probably unhealthy or slow. Check backend CPU/memory; one may be OOMing under load. (3) **Check backend connection pool** — backends often have a max connection limit (e.g., Tomcat's `maxThreads=200`); if all threads are busy, new requests queue and NGINX times out. Increase the backend pool or add more instances. (4) **Check NGINX upstream config** — `proxy_connect_timeout`, `proxy_read_timeout`, `proxy_next_upstream` should be set so NGINX retries on a different backend instead of returning 502. (5) **Check keep-alive** — `keepalive` in the upstream block reuses connections; without it NGINX opens a new TCP connection per request, which exhausts backend ports under load. (6) **Monitor backend latency percentiles** — if p99 backend response time spikes to 5 seconds during peak, NGINX's `proxy_read_timeout` (default 60s) is fine but the queue is the bottleneck. The most common cause I have seen: backend maxThreads too low for peak QPS, fixed by either raising maxThreads or adding instances.
**Visual:**
```
Debugging ladder:
  1. tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log    (which backend, why)
  2. curl http://backend-1:8080/health    (direct backend health)
  3. check backend CPU/memory (top, free)  (one OOMing?)
  4. check backend connection pool stats  (all threads busy?)
  5. check NGINX upstream timeouts        (proxy_read_timeout = ?)
  6. check NGINX keepalive config         (keepalive 32; in upstream block)
  7. monitor p99 backend response time    (spike during peak?)
```

### Q2. You want to deploy a new version of your API with 5% of traffic going to the new version, ramping to 100% over 2 hours. How do you configure the reverse proxy?
**Answer:** Use weighted routing in the reverse proxy. NGINX upstream: `server backend-v1:8080 weight=95; server backend-v2:8080 weight=5;`. AWS ALB: two target groups (v1-tg, v2-tg) with weighted routing rules (95/5). Envoy/Istio: a VirtualService with weighted destinations (v1: 95, v2: 5). Ramp sequence: 5% -> 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%, holding each step for 10–15 minutes while monitoring error rate, latency, and business metrics. If error rate exceeds threshold (e.g., 1% 5xx), abort the rollout by flipping weights back to 100/0. Critical guardrails: (1) Health-check both versions independently — a failing v2 backend should be removed automatically. (2) Monitor business metrics (conversion rate, error rate) not just infrastructure metrics — a v2 that returns 200 but breaks checkout is worse than a v2 that 500s. (3) Use sticky sessions if the v2 has schema changes that are incompatible with v1 (otherwise a user could hit v1 then v2 mid-session and get inconsistent state). (4) Have a fast rollback — keep v1 running at full capacity for the entire ramp so you can flip back in seconds. (5) For finer control, use Istio's traffic splitting with HTTP-header-based rules (route internal-test users' requests to v2 first). (6) Automate the ramp with a tool like Argo Rollouts or Flagger that watches metrics and auto-aborts on threshold breach.
**Visual:**
```
NGINX upstream (weighted):
  upstream api {
    server backend-v1:8080 weight=95;
    server backend-v2:8080 weight=5;
  }

Ramp schedule (with auto-abort on error rate > 1%):
  T+0:    95/5   (hold 10 min, monitor)
  T+10m:  90/10  (hold 10 min)
  T+20m:  75/25
  T+30m:  50/50
  T+45m:  25/75
  T+60m:  0/100  (v1 kept warm for rollback)
  T+90m:  decommission v1 if all metrics green
```

### Q3. Your reverse proxy becomes a single point of failure. How do you make it highly available?
**Answer:** Layer three patterns. (1) **Multiple proxy instances** — never run one NGINX; run at least 2 in an autoscaling group behind a cloud load balancer (AWS ALB in front of NGINX, or NGINX behind NLB for TCP pass-through). The cloud LB is itself HA (AWS ALB is a managed multi-AZ service). (2) **Multi-AZ deployment** — run proxies in at least 2 AZs (us-east-1a and us-east-1b); an AZ outage takes down half your capacity but the other half serves traffic. (3) **DNS-based failover** — for multi-region, run proxies in each region and use Route 53 health-checked failover: if us-east-1's proxies fail their health check, DNS returns the EU-West proxy IPs within TTL seconds. For self-managed NGINX without a cloud LB, use keepalived/VRRP — two NGINX instances share a virtual IP (VIP); the active one holds the VIP, and the standby takes over in <1 second if the active dies. The trade-off: every layer of HA adds cost and complexity. A common production setup: Route 53 → ALB (managed, multi-AZ) → NGINX/Envoy (autoscaling, multi-AZ) → backend (autoscaling, multi-AZ). This gives you 99.99% availability with no single point of failure. Netflix's Zuul gateway runs in this pattern across 3 regions with Route 53 failover.
**Visual:**
```
Single proxy (SPOF):
  client -> [NGINX] -> backend
  (NGINX down = entire site down)

HA pattern:
  client -> Route 53 (DNS failover, TTL=60)
            |
            +-> us-east ALB (managed, multi-AZ)
            |     |
            |     +-> NGINX-1a, NGINX-1b, NGINX-1c  (autoscaling)
            |          |
            |          +-> backend-1a, backend-1b, backend-1c
            |
            +-> eu-west ALB (managed, multi-AZ)   <-- failover target
                  |
                  +-> NGINX-2a, NGINX-2b, NGINX-2c
                       |
                       +-> backend-2a, backend-2b, backend-2c
```

### Q4. You are running NGINX in front of an API. The API team wants to deploy a new endpoint that requires 30 seconds to respond (large report generation). NGINX returns 504 after 60 seconds. How do you configure?
**Answer:** NGINX has several timeouts that need tuning for long-running requests. (1) `proxy_read_timeout` — default 60s, time NGINX waits for the backend to send the response; raise to 120s for the report endpoint. (2) `proxy_send_timeout` — time between two writes to the backend; default 60s. (3) `proxy_connect_timeout` — time to establish the connection; default 60s but should be much lower (5–10s) so NGINX fails fast to a healthy backend. (4) `keepalive_timeout` — client-side keep-alive; default 75s, usually fine. Configure per-location: `location /reports { proxy_read_timeout 120s; proxy_pass http://api; }`. But 30-second synchronous requests are a bad pattern — the client ties up a connection for 30 seconds, the proxy holds a backend thread for 30 seconds, and at scale you exhaust resources. The better pattern: make the report generation async. (1) Client `POST /reports` -> backend returns `202 Accepted` with a `Location: /reports/12345/status` URL. (2) Client polls `GET /reports/12345/status` every few seconds; backend returns `202 Pending` or `303 See Other` with the final URL when done. (3) Or use webhooks: client provides a callback URL, backend POSTs the result when ready. (4) Or use Server-Sent Events / WebSocket to stream progress. Netflix's report endpoints all use the async pattern; synchronous 30s requests would melt the API gateway under load.
**Visual:**
```
Bad pattern (synchronous 30s request):
  client --request--> NGINX --request--> backend
       (holds conn 30s)      (holds thread 30s)
  At 1000 RPS = 30,000 concurrent threads. Melts backend.

Better pattern (async polling):
  client POST /reports -> NGINX -> backend
  backend returns 202 + Location: /reports/12345/status
  client GET /reports/12345/status (every 5s)
    backend returns 202 Pending until done
    then 303 See Other + Location: /reports/12345/result
  client GET /reports/12345/result -> 200 + body

NGINX still needs proxy_read_timeout 120s as a safety net,
but most requests complete in <100ms.
```

### Q5. You want to add rate limiting to your API: 100 requests per minute per API key. Where do you implement it — at the reverse proxy or in the application?
**Answer:** Implement at the reverse proxy for the bulk of the protection, with the application as a second line of defense. At the proxy: NGINX has `limit_req_zone` (token bucket per key) and `limit_req` directives; Envoy has rate limit filters that call an external rate limit service; AWS ALB doesn't have native rate limiting but CloudFront/WAF does. The proxy reads the API key from the `X-API-Key` header or JWT, hashes it, and increments a counter in a shared zone (NGINX shared memory, Redis for distributed Envoy). If the counter exceeds 100/minute, the proxy returns `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After: 60` — without touching the backend. Benefits: backend CPU is protected from flood traffic; the proxy can handle 100,000 RPS of rate-limit checks vs the backend's 10,000 RPS of business logic. Trade-offs: (1) The proxy rate limit is per-instance unless you use a shared store (Redis); for accurate limits across N proxies, you need a distributed counter. (2) The proxy sees the API key in the header — make sure your logging does not capture it. (3) Complex rules (e.g., "100/min for free tier, 10000/min for paid") require the proxy to know the tier, which means a lookup. The application should also enforce rate limits as a defense-in-depth measure, because a misconfigured proxy or a direct-to-backend path (e.g., internal traffic) should not bypass limits. Stripe and GitHub both enforce rate limits at the edge (proxy/CDN) and in the application.
**Visual:**
```
Edge rate limit (proxy):
  client -> NGINX -> limit_req zone=api_key:10r/m burst=20
            |
            v
          shared memory (or Redis for multi-proxy)
          {key_abc: 47/100, key_def: 92/100, ...}
            |
            v
          if over limit -> 429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After: 60
          (backend never sees the request)

Application rate limit (defense in depth):
  app middleware: check rate limit for this API key
  (catches direct-to-backend traffic, internal abusers)
```

### Q6. You are adopting a service mesh (Istio). How do you migrate 50 microservices from NGINX-to-NGINX direct calls to Envoy sidecars with mTLS?
**Answer:** The migration is a multi-quarter project, not a flag flip. Phase 1: install the Istio control plane (Istiod) in PERMISSIVE mode — services accept both mTLS and plaintext, so you can add sidecars gradually without breaking anything. Phase 2: add sidecars to a few non-critical services first; verify traffic flows correctly and metrics appear in the Istio dashboard (Kiali). Phase 3: instrument each service's traffic to confirm what is actually mTLS-encrypted. Phase 4: switch services one at a time to STRICT mode using PeerAuthentication; if anything breaks, flip back to PERMISSIVE. Phase 5: for each service, define AuthorizationPolicies that specify which callers can call which endpoints (e.g., "billing can call orders but not auth"). Phase 6: migrate the inter-service traffic from NGINX-to-NGINX to sidecar-to-sidecar — the sidecars take over mTLS, retries, timeouts, and traffic splitting; NGINX is now only the edge (client-facing) proxy. Phase 7: after all services are on sidecars, decommission the inter-service NGINX proxies. The biggest pitfalls: (1) services that do not propagate trace headers break distributed tracing; (2) services with very high request rates see CPU overhead from the sidecar (~5%); (3) a misconfigured AuthorizationPolicy can block critical traffic — always test in PERMISSIVE first. Netflix, Airbnb, and Square have all done this migration over 12–18 months.
**Visual:**
```
Phase 1 (PERMISSIVE, sidecars added gradually):
  billing (sidecar) --mTLS--> orders (sidecar)
                       |
                       +--plaintext (still accepted)
  orders (no sidecar) --plaintext--> auth (no sidecar)

Phase 4 (STRICT service-by-service):
  billing --mTLS--> orders --mTLS--> auth
  AuthorizationPolicy: billing can call orders
                       orders can call auth
                       billing CANNOT call auth (deny)

Phase 6 (sidecars fully adopted, NGINX becomes edge only):
  client -> NGINX (edge) -> Envoy ingress -> Envoy sidecars -> backends
  Inter-service NGINX proxies decommissioned.
```

### Q7. You need to migrate from NGINX to Envoy as your reverse proxy. How do you do it safely?
**Answer:** The migration is similar to a CDN migration: run both in parallel, shift traffic gradually. (1) **Stand up Envoy as a parallel proxy** with identical config (same TLS certs, same backend pool, same routing rules, same health checks). Envoy config is YAML with listeners, clusters, routes, and endpoints — quite different from NGINX's directives, so use a tool like `nginx2envoy` or hand-translate. (2) **Test with a canary hostname** — point `test.example.com` at Envoy and verify byte-for-byte identical responses vs NGINX. Diff headers, status codes, response bodies, timing. (3) **DNS-based weighted cutover** — `api.example.com CNAME nginx-endpoint` (weight 95) and `api.example.com CNAME envoy-endpoint` (weight 5). Route 53 weighted routing lets you shift traffic 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 95% -> 100% over a few days. (4) **Monitor** error rate, latency, cache hit ratio, TLS handshake latency. Envoy and NGINX have slightly different defaults (e.g., Envoy's default keep-alive is different) that can cause subtle issues. (5) **Keep NGINX running for rollback** for at least 1 week after cutover. (6) **Decommission NGINX** once Envoy has run cleanly for a week. Common gotchas: (a) Envoy's default `retry_on` is more aggressive than NGINX's, which can amplify load on backends; tune it. (b) Envoy's access log format differs from NGINX's, so your log analysis tools need updates. (c) Envoy's xDS dynamic config requires a control plane (Istiod, or your own) — make sure you have one before going to production. Lyft migrated from NGINX to Envoy in 2016–2017 and open-sourced the result; their migration took ~6 months.
**Visual:**
```
T-0:   test.example.com -> Envoy (canary, verify diffs vs NGINX)
T-1d:  api.example.com Route 53 weighted: 95% NGINX, 5% Envoy
T-2d:  75% NGINX, 25% Envoy  (monitor errors, latency)
```

quiz.explanation: A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers and accepts incoming client requests, forwarding them to one of several backends, then returning the response to the client. The client thinks it is talking to the server; the server thinks it is talking to a client; neither knows the proxy is there. Use cases: load balancing, TLS termination, caching, rate limiting, routing, observability.

quiz.explanation: TLS termination means the reverse proxy holds the TLS certificate, completes the TLS handshake with the client, decrypts incoming TLS records, and forwards the resulting plaintext HTTP to the backend over a private network. Benefits: (1) CPU offload — asymmetric crypto (RSA/ECDSA signatures) is expensive; consolidating it on the proxy lets backends focus on application logic.

quiz.explanation: Active health checks are the proxy periodically polling each backend's health endpoint (e.g., GET /health every 5 seconds) and removing unhealthy backends from the pool. NGINX's health_check interval=5s fails=3 passes=2, AWS ALB's target group health checks, and Envoy's active health checks all do this. The trade-off: 5-second polling means a backend can serve traffic for up to 5 seconds after it fails.
